one_liner: Go codegen tool producing reflection-free struct JSON marshalers; README (2016) shows ~2.8x marshal, ~5.7x unmarshal vs encoding/json.
what_it_does: Replaces encoding/json's runtime reflection with generated code. You run `easyjson -all file.go` (or mark structs with `//easyjson:json`) and it writes `file_easyjson.go` with MarshalEasyJSON/UnmarshalEasyJSON plus std-compatible MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON methods. You then call easyjson.Marshal/Unmarshal, MarshalToWriter or MarshalToHTTPResponseWriter instead of json.Marshal, and regenerate whenever the structs change. The generator also adds options the stdlib lacks: snake_case/lowerCamelCase naming, omitempty by default, disallow_unknown_fields, `intern`/`nocopy` string tags, and `opt.*` optional-value wrappers.
how_it_is_fast: Ahead-of-time code generation gives each struct straight-line encode/decode code. JSON field prefixes such as `,"name":` are baked in as string constants, and decoding picks a field with a Go `switch` on the key, so nothing uses reflection or looks up a field cache at runtime. Decoding goes through jlexer, a pull tokenizer driven by generated code that already knows which type comes next. It finds string ends with bytes.IndexByte and turns keys into strings with an unsafe zero-copy []byte-to-string cast. Encoding appends into a chain of chunks (128 B growing to 32 KB; chunks of 512 B or more are recycled per size class through sync.Pool), and DumpTo writes that chain out as net.Buffers without first joining it into one slice, which is why writer mode posts the best numbers.
when_to_use: High-QPS Go services that encode and decode a fixed set of known structs (API request/response types), where you control the build and can commit generated *_easyjson.go files.

Responses written straight to an http.ResponseWriter or io.Writer (MarshalToHTTPResponseWriter/MarshalToWriter). The README's largest gains are in writer mode: 263 vs 75 MB/s single-goroutine, 1748 vs 252 MB/s concurrent.

Frequent small messages where allocations dominate. The README's 80-byte unmarshal is 3 allocs/128 B vs 14 allocs/720 B for encoding/json, and writer-mode marshal of the 13 KB doc is 8 allocs/742 B vs 9 allocs/23 KB.
Payloads with repeated low-cardinality string values (the `intern` tag deduplicates them) or short-lived decoded objects (the `nocopy` tag skips string copies).
Pure-Go deployments on any GOARCH, including environments that forbid unsafe (App Engine disables it automatically, or build with `easyjson_nounsafe`).
when_not_to_use: Generic struct types: codegen fails or emits uncompilable code (issue #369, open since 2022; #414 'cannot use generic type ... without instantiation'). Types in `package main` are also unsupported, because the generator must import the package through a `go run` bootstrap.

When output or behavior must match encoding/json exactly. Map keys come out in Go map iteration order, not sorted (#292), so output is not byte-stable. Object keys match case-sensitively. Floats use strconv 'g' formatting, so 1e6 comes out as `1e+06` (#425). []byte fields accept only base64, not integer arrays (#434).
Large or unbounded input you want to stream: jlexer works only on an in-memory []byte, and UnmarshalFromReader ReadAlls the whole body. The README says there is no true streaming encode either.

Strict validation of untrusted input: string tokens are scanned only for their closing quote, so control characters and invalid UTF-8 in strings are not rejected on decode. The README says full validation is not done.
Dynamic data (`interface{}`/`map[string]interface{}` fields): the generated encoder falls back to encoding/json.Marshal for interface values that have no marshaler, so those parts get no speedup.

integration.form: module (Go package plus an `easyjson` codegen CLI that writes *_easyjson.go source files)
integration.dependencies: github.com/josharian/intern (runtime); a full Go toolchain at generation time (generator shells out to `go run`)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.20 per go.mod; CI tests only Go 1.23
integration.platforms: any Go target (pure Go; unsafe is optional). CI runs only on ubuntu-latest; the arm64 CI job is commented out
integration.thread_safety: Not formally documented. Each call builds its own jlexer.Lexer/jwriter.Writer and only the sync.Pool-backed chunk pool is shared, so concurrent calls on distinct values are safe; the README's concurrent benchmarks rely on this. buffer.Init() must run before any marshaling.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the generated MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON satisfy json.Marshaler/json.Unmarshaler, so existing json.Marshal calls keep working. Most of the speedup, though, needs a codegen step plus calls to easyjson.Marshal/Unmarshal, and keys, map order and float formatting differ from encoding/json.

gotchas: Calling the stdlib json.Marshal/json.Unmarshal on generated types goes through MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON. The README warns this carries a 'significant performance penalty' compared with easyjson.Marshal/Unmarshal, so switch the call sites.

With the `nocopy` tag, decoded strings point into the input buffer through an unsafe cast. Reusing or mutating that []byte (for example a pooled read buffer) silently corrupts them, and one retained string keeps the whole input alive.
Marshaling a struct whose embedded struct pointer is nil panics (#368, open). The decoder always allocates embedded pointer fields with new().

Current code differs from the 2016 README. SkipRecursive now runs encoding/json's json.Valid on skipped unknown fields and RawMessage subtrees, so passing large raw sub-documents through pays for stdlib validation (#387). Issue #359 reports that since Go 1.17, DumpTo/MarshalToWriter no longer returns chunks to the pool, and that code is unchanged at HEAD. Re-benchmark on your own Go version.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick easyjson over go-json, jsoniter or Sonic when you can add a codegen step and want reflection-free, pure-Go marshalers with the fewest allocations on known structs, especially when writing straight to an http.ResponseWriter. Pick go-json (its README lists itself as fully encoding/json-compatible and easyjson as not) or jsoniter when you need an import swap with no generated files, generic types, or byte-identical encoding/json behavior. The sibling ratios come from different benchmarks, so don't compare them directly.
verified_claims_summary: The README tables set encoding/json against easyjson-generated code on a 13 KB Twitter search response, an 80-byte fragment and a ~500 KB 50-copy struct: unmarshal 125 vs 22 MB/s (~5.7x); single-goroutine marshal 213 vs 75 MB/s (~2.8x), or 263 MB/s (~3.5x) when easyjson writes to a discard writer, compared with std json.Marshal rather than json.Encoder. No CPU or flags are given, and the only Go version stated is go1.6 for the 2016 ffjson/codec runs. In the HEAD benchmark code, the concurrent 'regular' easyjson marshal credits the 13,024-byte whitespace-included input file per op while encoding/json is credited its ~9 KB output, which would inflate that 792 vs 252 MB/s (~3.1x) ratio by about 1.4x.
status_note: Maintained but slow-moving: v0.9.2 (2026-03-14, added omitzero) followed v0.9.1 (2025-09), with ~100 open issues/PRs including 2022-era generics support; MIT, pure Go, and easy to vendor.
